---
title: "Different outcomes"
subtitle: "Example 6.4 of Mize, Doan, and Long (2019)"
---

The same predictors can have different effects on different outcomes. Here two
negative binomial models predict days of poor mental health and days of poor
physical health from the same set of variables, and `mecompare` tests whether
each predictor matters more for one outcome than the other. With no variable
listed before the comma, `mecompare` computes marginal effects for every 
predictor in the models.

```{.stata-run}
. use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss_cme", clear
(gss_cme.dta | GSS 1972 - 2016 Weighted | 2018-07-10)

. drop if missing(mntlhlth, physhlth, woman, married, age, faminc, race, college, parent, reltrad)
(57,404 observations deleted)

. 
. quietly nbreg mntlhlth i.woman i.married i.parent i.college c.age faminc i.race i.year, vce(robust
> )

. estimates store mental

. 
. quietly nbreg physhlth i.woman i.married i.parent i.college c.age faminc i.race i.year, vce(robust
> )

. estimates store physical

```

For the count models the marginal effects are changes in the predicted rate
(expected number of days). Continuous predictors are changed by one standard
deviation:

Women report more poor physical health days, and more poor mental health days, 
than do men. The effect of gender is similar in size and not statistically 
significantly different across the two outcomes.

Married individuals report fewer poor mental health days than do the unmarried. 
Marriage has no significant effect on poor physical health days. The cross-model 
difference is significant, indicating a larger effect of marriage on mental than
